title: iPhone 18 Pro Launch, pricey Refurbished iPhone 17 Pros, Galaxy Z8 Foldables Discounted – GSMArena News
body:
Apple’s latest flagship devices have finally hit store shelves, with the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max now available for purchase across the United States and 64 additional markets. While the new models are drawing long queues and hefty price tags, the launch has also highlighted an unexpected twist in the premium‑phone market: refurbished iPhone 17 Pro Max units are being sold at prices that match their brand‑new counterparts. At the same time, Samsung is pushing a steep discount on its upcoming Galaxy Z8 foldable, aiming to capture bargain‑hungry consumers eager for high‑end foldable technology. The contrasting pricing strategies from the two tech giants underscore a shifting landscape where premium devices are both more accessible and, paradoxically, more expensive than ever.

Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro line arrives with a suite of incremental upgrades that build on the success of the previous generation. The devices feature a new titanium‑reinforced frame, a brighter always‑on display, and a 48‑megapixel main sensor that promises superior low‑light performance. Under the hood, Apple has introduced its A19 Bionic chip, delivering a claimed 15 percent boost in CPU speed and a 20 percent increase in GPU efficiency. Battery life has been nudged upward by roughly an hour, thanks to a combination of a larger cell and the more power‑savvy silicon. Pricing starts at $999 for the 128 GB iPhone 18 Pro and $1,199 for the 256 GB iPhone 18 Pro Max, placing the devices firmly in the premium tier.

What makes the launch noteworthy, however, is the price parity observed in the refurbished market. Certified‑refurbished iPhone 17 Pro Max units, which were introduced just a year ago, are now listed on Apple’s own refurbishment program at $1,199 for the 256 GB model—the same price as a brand‑new iPhone 18 Pro Max with identical storage. This phenomenon reflects both the scarcity of newer inventory and the high resale value Apple devices retain. Analysts suggest that the limited supply of the iPhone 18 Pro series, compounded by production bottlenecks in key components such as the new camera modules, has driven demand for older‑generation phones, allowing Apple’s refurbishment program to command premium prices.

Samsung’s response to the high‑end smartphone market comes in the form of a deep discount on its upcoming Galaxy Z8 foldable. The Z8, slated for release later this year, is positioned as a direct competitor to Apple’s Pro models, offering a 7.6‑inch dynamic AMOLED display that folds inward, a triple‑camera array, and a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor. Samsung has slashed the pre‑order price by roughly 15 percent, bringing the entry‑level configuration to $1,099. The aggressive pricing is intended to lure consumers who might otherwise gravitate toward Apple’s ecosystem, especially as the foldable segment matures and production costs begin to fall. Industry watchers note that Samsung’s discount strategy could set a new benchmark for foldable pricing, potentially accelerating mainstream adoption.

The divergent approaches of Apple and Samsung also reveal broader trends in consumer expectations. Apple’s strategy leans on brand loyalty and the allure of incremental innovation, banking on customers’ willingness to pay a premium for the latest design language and ecosystem integration. Samsung, meanwhile, appears to be betting on price elasticity, using discounts to lower the barrier to entry for a technology that has historically been viewed as a niche luxury. Both tactics are being tested against a backdrop of global supply chain volatility, inflationary pressures, and a growing secondary market for refurbished devices that blurs the line between new and used.

Looking ahead, the market will likely see intensified competition as other manufacturers introduce their own foldable and premium smartphones. Apple’s pricing of refurbished models could prompt a reevaluation of its trade‑in and refurbishment policies, possibly leading to more aggressive discounting of older devices to clear inventory. Samsung’s discount on the Z8 may force rivals to offer comparable deals, which could compress profit margins but expand the overall user base for foldable technology. For consumers, the immediate takeaway is clear: the premium smartphone segment is becoming both more exclusive and more accessible, depending on the brand and the channel through which the device is purchased. As the next wave of flagship phones looms on the horizon, the industry will watch closely how pricing, supply constraints, and consumer appetite shape the next chapter of high‑end mobile innovation.
